title: Hand Pain (Rheumatoid / Psoriatic Arthritis)
patient_instructions: You are Angela Rossi, a 40-year-old administrative assistant, presenting to your GP with pain in BOTH hands that has been getting worse over about three months. The pain and stiffness are worst first thing in the morning and last well over an hour; the joints loosen and feel better as you use them through the day - so it is worse with rest, better with movement. You have noticed swelling over your knuckles (the middle and base finger joints) on both hands, symmetrically. You feel generally tired and run-down. There is no rash on your elbows or knees, no recent diarrhoea, no genital discharge, no history of a hot single red joint, no relationship to alcohol or red meat, and no skin tanning. Your mother had 'arthritis'. It is affecting your typing and your job. IDEAS: you think it might be 'arthritis like my mum'. CONCERNS: you are worried about your hands becoming deformed and not being able to work. EXPECTATIONS: you want a diagnosis and to know if there is treatment. Affect: worried but cooperative. Volunteer the symmetry, morning stiffness >1 hour and improvement with movement readily; give the negative screening answers (rash, bowel, discharge, diet, tanning) only when asked.
candidate_instructions: You are the GP in an Australian general practice. Angela Rossi, a 40-year-old woman, presents with pain in both hands. In this 8-minute station: take a focused history (about 6 minutes), then examination and investigation findings will appear on screen - symmetrical swelling and tenderness across multiple finger joints (MCPs, PIPs) and wrists with sparing of the DIPs; rheumatoid factor positive, anti-CCP positive, raised CRP, and a mild normocytic anaemia (ANA weakly positive and urate mildly raised as distractors). Give the examiner your most likely diagnosis and differentials with reasons, and outline your initial management and referral plan. You do not need to perform a physical examination.
examiner_instructions: Reward a structured hand-pain history that identifies the inflammatory pattern (symmetrical, worse in the morning with prolonged stiffness, better with use) and systematically screens the differential groups: inflammatory/crystal arthritis (RA, psoriatic, gout, reactive/IBD), red flags (weight loss, fever, malignancy), neurological (cervical radiculopathy, carpal tunnel) and other (haemochromatosis, De Quervain's). The candidate should diagnose rheumatoid arthritis and know its distribution involves MCPs, PIPs and wrists symmetrically and SPARES the DIPs (DIP involvement suggests OA or psoriatic arthritis). On investigations, anti-CCP is highly specific and prognostic but is NOT confirmatory in isolation - diagnosis uses ACR/EULAR 2010 criteria (joint count, RF/anti-CCP, CRP/ESR, duration); the raised ANA and urate are distractors. For management expect EARLY rheumatology referral (within weeks) for a treat-to-target DMARD strategy (methotrexate first-line, PBS-subsidised) with baseline FBC/LFT/renal, and short-term NSAID/paracetamol or corticosteroid bridging. Prompt if needed: 'Which joints does RA typically spare?'

criteria: Structured pain history and identifies the inflammatory pattern (symmetrical, prolonged morning stiffness >30-60 min, better with use, worse with rest)
Systematically screens differential groups (RA, psoriatic, gout, reactive/IBD, OA) with targeted questions (rash, bowel, discharge/STI, diet, family history)
Screens neurological causes (cervical radiculopathy, carpal tunnel - nocturnal pins-and-needles, shaking hands) and other causes (haemochromatosis - tanning, fatigue)
Screens red flags (weight loss, fever/chills, lumps) and functional/occupational impact
Diagnoses rheumatoid arthritis with reasons and states the typical distribution: symmetrical MCPs, PIPs and wrists with DIP sparing
Correctly weights investigations - anti-CCP strongly supports (highly specific/prognostic) but does not confirm in isolation; diagnosis uses ACR/EULAR 2010 criteria
Identifies the raised ANA and urate as distractors and offers relevant differentials (psoriatic arthritis, gout, OA, reactive arthritis)
Arranges EARLY (within weeks) rheumatology referral for a treat-to-target DMARD strategy to prevent erosive joint damage
Names methotrexate as first-line PBS-subsidised DMARD and orders baseline FBC/LFT/renal before commencing

Provides symptomatic bridging (NSAID/paracetamol or short corticosteroid) and appropriate first-line investigation bundle (FBC, CRP/ESR, RF, anti-CCP, urate, hand X-rays); recognises a hot single joint would need urgent aspiration to exclude sepsis
Clear empathic lay explanation of RA as an autoimmune joint inflammation and why early treatment matters
Addresses the patient's concerns about deformity and work and agrees a follow-up plan

red_flags: Hot, swollen single joint with fever - exclude septic arthritis with urgent joint aspiration; do not dismiss as inflammatory
Constitutional features (weight loss, fever, night sweats, lumps) suggesting malignancy or infection
Progressive neurological signs / thenar wasting in carpal tunnel indicating need for urgent decompression
Untreated inflammatory arthritis risks rapid erosive joint damage - delay in DMARD therapy is itself a red flag
australian_guidelines: ACR/EULAR 2010 classification criteria (used in Australian practice) - RA diagnosis combines joint count, serology (RF and anti-CCP), acute-phase reactants (CRP/ESR) and symptom duration; anti-CCP is specific/prognostic, not confirmatory alone

eTG / RACGP - early referral (ideally within weeks) to a rheumatologist for a treat-to-target DMARD strategy; methotrexate is first-line and PBS-subsidised, with NSAID/paracetamol or short corticosteroid bridging
eTG - baseline FBC, LFTs and renal function before commencing methotrexate, with ongoing monitoring

PBS - biologic and conventional DMARDs (e.g. methotrexate) are subsidised for RA meeting criteria; carpal tunnel managed with nocturnal splint, activity modification, corticosteroid injection or decompression
learning_objectives: Differentiate inflammatory (RA/psoriatic) from mechanical hand pain using pattern, distribution and stiffness duration
Recognise the RA joint distribution (symmetrical MCP/PIP/wrist with DIP sparing) and avoid confusing it with OA
Interpret RA serology correctly, including that anti-CCP supports but does not confirm, and identify distractor results
Apply the Australian early-DMARD treat-to-target pathway with appropriate baseline monitoring and referral
key_points: RA = symmetrical MCP + PIP + wrist involvement with DIP sparing; DIP involvement points to OA or psoriatic arthritis
Anti-CCP is highly specific and prognostically important but is not diagnostic in isolation - use ACR/EULAR 2010 criteria
Early DMARD therapy (methotrexate first-line, PBS-subsidised) within weeks prevents irreversible erosive damage

Psoriatic arthritis is suggested by dactylitis of the 2nd/3rd fingers plus an extensor-surface silvery-scaled rash; carpal tunnel and De Quervain's are non-arthritic mimics with specific tests (Tinel/Phalen; Finkelstein)

citations.claim: Gout is a key differential for hand/finger joint pain with a characteristic joint distribution and tendency to recur, supporting the case's gout screening questions.
Hand and thumb anatomy/assessment is a defined AMC clinical condition, anchoring the structured hand-examination framing used in the case.

Thyroid disease is systemically relevant to hand symptoms; the case correctly lists hypothyroidism among carpal tunnel associations (adjacent thyrotoxicosis-signs chunk supports the thyroid-hand link).
